# Accessories

*Advanced feature. Not covered in trial curriculum. Full documentation to be added post-launch.*

Accessory Sparks are Entity Sparks designed to attach to the player's body at runtime, typically used to build wrist-mounted UI in VR — a watch-style interface the player can glance at and interact with.

**Watch Band** — the visual strap component. Attaches to a specified body part (typically the left hand in VR) and aligns itself relative to the Watch Face. Set Is Attached to true in the Traits Panel or via behavior wiring to snap it to the player.

**Watch Face** — the interactive face of the watch. Also attaches to a body part via Is Attached. Supports a Billboard for displaying content and an "If Interacted" Effect for triggering actions when the player interacts with the watch — commonly used to open a menu or display status information.

### Shared Traits (Watch Band and Watch Face)

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Is Attached | When enabled, the Spark snaps to the player's body |
| Body Part | The body part to attach to (e.g., left hand) |
| Offset Position | Positional offset relative to the attachment point |
| Offset Rotation | Rotational offset relative to the attachment point |

title: Drawables
content:
# Drawables

*Advanced feature. Not covered in trial curriculum. Full documentation to be added post-launch.*

Drawable Sparks enable freehand drawing directly in the scene at runtime. The system consists of three cooperating Spark types:

**Drawable Surface** — a blank canvas Entity Spark that can be drawn on by a Marker Spark. Multiple Markers can draw on the same surface.

**Marker** — the drawing instrument. When it contacts a Drawable Surface, it renders a stroke. Configurable for color, pen size, stroke smoothness, and drawing distance. The Require Held trait controls whether the player must physically hold the Marker to draw, or whether it draws automatically on contact. A Marker can be attached invisibly to another Spark (with its color alpha set to 0 and Require Held unchecked) to allow non-Marker Sparks to draw on surfaces.

**Eraser** — removes strokes from a Drawable Surface one continuous stroke at a time.

### Key Marker Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Pen Color | RGBA color of the ink |
| Pen Size | Width of the stroke |
| Distance Between Points | Spacing between stroke points — lower values produce smoother curves (default: 0.01) |
| Require Held | When enabled, player must grip the Marker to draw; when disabled, draws on contact automatically |
| Max Drawing Distance | Maximum range at which the Marker renders on a surface (default: 0.03) |

title: Entity Spark Behaviors
content:
# Entity Spark Behaviors

All Entity Spark Instances share the same set of Causes and Effects. This page documents those behaviors. For Config Spark and Symbol Spark behaviors, see their individual reference pages. For Modifier behaviors (available in every Chapter), see [Modifiers](../modifiers/).

For an overview of how the Behaviors tab works, see [Behaviors tab](../ui-panels/behaviors-tab/).

---

## Causes

Causes are triggers. When a Cause's conditions are met, it fires its output and passes the signal downstream.

### Common Parameters

**One Shot**
Available on Approached, Collided, and Grabbed. When enabled, the Cause fires once — the first time its conditions are met — and then permanently deactivates for the remainder of the Chapter session. Use One Shot when an event should only happen once per session, such as playing an introductory animation.

**Prerequisite traits**
Some Causes require a corresponding trait to be enabled on the Instance before they can fire. If the prerequisite trait is not enabled, the Cause will never trigger. Builder displays a yellow warning triangle on a Cause node when it detects a missing prerequisite — but this warning is not consistently applied across all Causes. Always verify relevant traits in the Traits Panel directly. See [Warning Triangle Inconsistency](#warning-triangle-inconsistency) in the Notes section.

---

### On Started

> **Advanced.** On Started works in conjunction with Clone. If you have not used Clone before, start there first.

Fires when this Entity is spawned by a Clone Effect. Use it to trigger behavior on the cloned instance at the moment it appears in the scene — for example, starting an animation, setting a trait, or launching a timer on a newly spawned object.

No configurable parameters.

**One output.**

---

### Approached

Fires when the player or a specified Spark Instance enters within a set distance of this Entity.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Distance | The proximity radius that triggers the Cause, in scene units (approximately meters) | 5 |
| Player | When enabled (X), fires when the player enters the zone | Enabled |
| Spark | When a Spark Instance is selected from the dropdown, also fires when that Instance enters the zone | None |
| One Shot | Fire once only | Disabled |

Both Player and Spark can be active simultaneously — the Cause fires when either condition is met.

**One output.**

---

### Collided

Fires when this Entity collides with another object in the scene.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| On Enter | Fire when the collision begins | Enabled |
| On Exit | Fire when the collision ends | Disabled |
| With Player | Fire when the collision involves the player | Enabled |
| With Spark | Fire when the collision involves a specific Spark Instance | Disabled |
| Left Hand | Fire specifically for left controller hand collisions | Disabled |
| Right Hand | Fire specifically for right controller hand collisions | Disabled |
| Threshold | Minimum time delay in seconds before a new collision can be registered after an initial detection | 0.1 |
| One Shot | Fire once only | Disabled |

**Threshold** prevents double-triggers from a single collision event. Increase it if you are seeing unintended repeated triggers.

**Prerequisite:** Is Collidable must be enabled in the Traits Panel. **Builder does not show a warning triangle when Is Collidable is disabled.** A Collided Cause with Is Collidable off will fail silently. Always verify Is Collidable when Collided is not behaving as expected.

**Held Sparks trigger collisions.** A Spark that the player is currently holding (grabbed) can still trigger Collided events when it makes contact with other objects. This means you can wire behaviors that respond to the player hitting something with a held object.

**One output.**

---

### Grabbed

Fires when this Entity is picked up or put down by the player.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| One Shot | Fire once only | Disabled |

**Two outputs:**
- **Left output (On Grabbed):** fires when the player picks up the Entity
- **Right output (On Released):** fires when the player puts the Entity down

**Prerequisite:** Is Grabbable must be enabled in the Traits Panel. Builder shows a warning triangle when Is Grabbable is disabled.

**Grab direction constraint:** The player can only grab Sparks that are in front of them. A Spark directly behind the player cannot be picked up, even if it is within range and Is Grabbable is enabled.

---

### Interacted

Fires when the player activates this Entity. In VR, activation uses the laser pointer. In Builder play mode, press **E** while facing the object to simulate interaction.

No configurable parameters.

**Two outputs:**
- **Left output (Interact On):** fires when the player activates the Entity
- **Right output (Interact Off):** fires when the player deactivates the Entity

**Prerequisite:** Is Interactable must be enabled in the Traits Panel. Builder shows a warning triangle when Is Interactable is disabled.

> **Builder play mode distance limit:** You must be within approximately 1 meter of an object to interact with it in Builder play mode. This is more restrictive than VR. If pressing E does nothing, move closer and try again.

---

### Trait Is…

Fires when a specified trait on this Entity meets a defined condition.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Trait | The trait to evaluate — select from this Instance's exposed traits |
| Condition | Equal To, Greater Than, or Less Than |
| Value | The value to compare against |

Greater Than and Less Than are only meaningful for numeric traits. For boolean traits, use Equal To.

**One output.**

---

## Effects

Effects are consequences. When wired to a Cause output, an Effect executes when the Cause fires.

---

### Animation

#### Animate Play

Starts a named animation on this Entity.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Clip | The animation clip to play |
| Do Loop | When enabled, the animation loops continuously until stopped |

**Prerequisite:** The "Do Animation" trait must be enabled on this Spark Instance.

`[PENDING: confirm additional parameters (Material Name, Direction Obj., Speed) with developer]`

#### Animate Stop

Stops the currently playing animation on this Entity. No parameters.

---

### Attachment and Grab

#### Attach On

Attaches this Entity to another Spark Instance as a child object.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Type | What to attach to: **Spark**, **Player_Head**, **Player_Hand_L**, **Player_Hand_R** | Spark |
| Parent | When Type is Spark: the specific Spark Instance to attach to | None |
| Offset Position X/Y/Z | Position offset from the attachment point's origin, in the **parent's local space** | 0, 0, 0 |
| Offset Rotation X/Y/Z | Rotation offset from the attachment point's orientation, in the **parent's local space** | 0, 0, 0 |

> **Note:** Offset Position and Offset Rotation are applied in the parent object's local coordinate space, not Builder's world space. The effective direction of each axis depends on the parent's rotation. For an unrotated parent: X = Builder X, Y = Altitude, Z = Builder Y. This is a known bug — see [GitHub issue #65](https://github.com/PixoVR/bonfire-pixovr/issues/65).

#### Attach Off

Detaches this Entity from its current parent and returns it to world space. No parameters.

#### Force Grab

Places this Entity directly into the player's hand without requiring the player to pick it up manually.

`[PENDING: confirm whether Left/Right hand is configurable and where that parameter appears]`

#### Force Drop

Removes this Entity from the player's hand. No parameters.

---

### Appearance

#### Highlight

Adds or removes a pulsing blue highlight on this Entity.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Enabled | Checked = highlight on; unchecked = highlight off | Unchecked |

**This is a state-setter, not a toggle.** See [Visible and Highlight Are State-Setters](#visible-and-highlight-are-state-setters) in the Notes section.

#### Visible

Shows or hides this Entity.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Enabled | Checked = visible; unchecked = hidden | Unchecked |

**This is a state-setter, not a toggle.**

> **Hidden objects cannot be interacted with.** A hidden Entity (Visible = off) will not respond to the "Interacted" Cause. Do not wire an "Interacted" Cause to a "Visible (off)" Effect expecting the player to interact with the hidden object to make it reappear — the interaction will never fire. Use a separate always-visible trigger object, or a different Cause such as "Approached". See [Toggle: Flip Between Two States](../../../wiring-behaviors/common-patterns/#toggle-flip-between-two-states) for the correct pattern.

#### Sub Mesh

Shows or hides a named submesh within this Entity's 3D model.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| SubMesh | The name of the submesh to affect | (first available) |
| Visible | Checked = show submesh; unchecked = hide submesh | Unchecked |

Requires the Entity's source asset to have defined named submeshes.

---

### Transform

#### Move

Moves this Entity to a target position.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Set Altitude | When enabled, this node sets the Entity's vertical position | Enabled |
| Altitude | Target altitude value | 0 |
| Set Position | When enabled, this node sets the Entity's horizontal position | Enabled |
| Position X | Target horizontal position — X axis | 0 |
| Position Y | Target horizontal position — Y axis | 0 |
| Move Type | Absolute: move to a specific coordinate. Relative: move by an offset | Absolute |
| Time To Move | Duration of the movement in seconds | 1 |

#### Rotate

Rotates this Entity to a target orientation.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Rotation X | Target X-axis rotation in degrees | 0 |
| Rotation Y | Target Y-axis rotation in degrees | 0 |
| Rotation Z | Target Z-axis rotation in degrees | 0 |
| Rotate Type | Absolute or Relative | Absolute |
| Time to Move | Duration of the rotation in seconds | 1 |

#### Scale

Scales this Entity uniformly. A single float value is applied equally to all axes — you cannot scale X, Y, and Z independently with this Effect.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Scale | Uniform scale multiplier applied to all axes | 1 |

---

### Logic and Conditions

#### Modify

Sets the value of any exposed trait on this Entity.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Trait | The trait to modify |
| Value | The new value |

#### If Trait Is…

A conditional gate. Passes the signal through only if the specified condition on this Instance is currently true.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Trait | The trait to evaluate |
| Condition | Equal To, Greater Than, or Less Than |
| Value | The value to compare against |

**One output** — fires only when the condition evaluates to true.

#### Interactable

Enables or disables user interaction with this Entity.

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Enabled | Checked = interactable; unchecked = not interactable | Unchecked |

---

### Lifecycle

#### Destroy

Removes this Entity Instance from the scene permanently for the remainder of the session. No parameters. Reloading the Chapter restores destroyed Instances.

#### Clone

> **Advanced.** Clone introduces runtime-generated Instances, which behave differently from Instances placed in the scene at authoring time. Use with care — cloned Instances are not visible in the Map Explorer or Instances pane and can be difficult to debug.

Creates a new Instance of this Entity Spark in the scene at runtime. Use Clone to dynamically add objects during play — spawning projectiles, populating a scene based on player actions, or creating multiple copies of an object.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Spawn Point | Where the clone appears: **Current** — at the Entity's current position; **Original** — at the Entity's original edit-mode position; **Custom** — at a manually specified position |
| Altitude | *(Custom only)* Vertical position of the spawn point |
| Position X / Y | *(Custom only)* Horizontal position of the spawn point |
| Rotation X / Y / Z | *(Custom only)* Rotation of the spawned clone |

---

## Notes

### Warning Triangle Inconsistency

Builder shows a yellow warning triangle on Grabbed and Interacted when Is Grabbable or Is Interactable is disabled. **Collided does not show this warning when Is Collidable is disabled.** A Collided Cause with Is Collidable off will fail silently. Always verify Is Collidable directly in the Traits Panel.

---

### Visible and Highlight Are State-Setters

Both Visible and Highlight set a fixed state — they do not toggle. To show and then hide the same Entity, you need two separate Visible nodes wired to different Causes: one checked, one unchecked. If you need a single node that flips between states on each fire, use Toggle upstream with two separate Effects.

---

### Grabbed and Interacted Have Two Outputs

| Cause | Left output | Right output |
|---|---|---|
| Grabbed | On Grabbed (entity picked up) | On Released (entity put down) |
| Interacted | Interact On (player activates) | Interact Off (player deactivates) |

Wire each output independently to drive separate behavior paths from the same Cause node.

---

*Pending items require developer confirmation before publishing. Search for `[PENDING` to find all unresolved entries.*

title: Environment Sparks
content:
# Environment Sparks

Environment Sparks are invisible Entity Sparks — they are visible in Builder but not to the player at runtime. They serve structural and interactive roles in a scene: defining where the player starts, where they can travel, and what areas trigger behavior.

Environment Sparks participate in behavior trees using the standard Entity Spark Causes and Effects documented in [Entity Spark Behaviors](entity-spark-behaviors/), unless noted otherwise below.

**Note:** Environment Sparks currently appear as a top-level folder in the Spark Browser alongside Entity Sparks. They are conceptually a subtype of Entity Spark.

---

## Light

A Light Spark adds a dynamic light source to the scene. It emits light from its position and can be adjusted for type, color temperature, and intensity.

### Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Type | **Point** — emits light in all directions from a single point. **Spot Light** — emits a cone of light, like a spotlight or flashlight. |
| Color Temperature | Adjusts the warmth or coolness of the light |
| Intensity | Controls the brightness of the light |

**Spot Light additional traits:**

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Direction | The direction the spotlight is pointing |
| Size Inner | The inner cone where light is at full intensity |
| Size Outer | The total spread of the spotlight beyond the inner cone |
| Range | How far the spotlight reaches |

---

## Portal

A Portal Spark is invisible to the player. It defines a destination point and teleports the player to that location when its "Teleport" Effect is triggered.

Common use: wire an "Approached" or "Collided" Cause on an invisible Trigger Spark to a Portal's "Teleport" Effect to create a seamless location transition.

### Effects

#### Teleport

Instantly moves the player to the Portal Spark's position.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Destination | The Spark Instance the player will be teleported to |

### Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Cooldown (s) | Wait time in seconds before the portal can be used again after teleportation (default: 0.5) |

> **Do not create mutual portal loops.** If Portal A teleports the player to Portal B, and Portal B is wired to teleport back to Portal A on the same collision trigger, the player will be teleported back and forth indefinitely. Always ensure portal destinations are one-directional, or add a gate (such as a State Machine or Interactable trigger) to control the return path.

> **Portal is invisible to players.** The Portal Spark does not render at runtime. Players have no visual indication that stepping into the area will teleport them. Add a visual cue at the portal entrance — a Billboard with instructions, a distinctively colored Primitive overlapping the zone, or a signpost — to communicate what the area does.

---

## Reflection Probe

A Reflection Probe Spark captures the surrounding environment and applies dynamic reflections to nearby shiny surfaces — glass, mirrors, polished metal, and similar materials. Moving the Reflection Probe updates which environment it captures.

Works best with high-fidelity (HiFi) assets. Low-poly assets benefit less from reflection probes.

### Traits

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|
| Size | Adjusts the range of the reflection capture |

---

## Spawn Point

A Spawn Point Spark defines where the player appears when the Chapter loads or restarts. Without a Spawn Point, the player spawns at the scene origin (position 0, 0, 0).

Each Chapter supports one Spawn Point. Place it at the intended starting position and orientation for the player.

No Causes, Effects, or additional traits beyond the base Entity Spark behaviors.

---

## Trigger

A Trigger Spark is an invisible, non-rendering Entity Spark that functions as a sensor zone. It supports the full set of standard Entity Spark Causes — particularly "Approached" and "Collided" — making it ideal for activating behavior when the player enters a designated area without any visible object in the scene.

Use a Trigger when you need spatial detection but do not want a visible object in the scene.

> **Trigger is invisible to players.** The Trigger Spark does not render at runtime. If you need players to know an area is interactive — that stepping into it will do something — add a visible element alongside it: a Billboard with instructions, a highlighted Primitive overlapping the zone, or any other indicator. The Trigger handles detection; the visual cue is a separate Spark.

No unique traits beyond the standard Entity Spark trait set.

title: Primitives
content:
# Primitives

Primitives are basic 3D shapes available in the Spark Browser. They behave as standard Entity Sparks — they have the full set of Entity Spark Causes, Effects, and Traits, and can participate in behavior trees like any other Entity Spark.

## Available Shapes

Cube, Sphere, Cylinder, Capsule, Plane, Quad, and others.

## Common Uses

**Prototyping and layout blocking** — Place Primitives to define spatial layout before final assets are imported. Swap with production assets when ready.

**Invisible collision boundaries** — Set Is Visible to off and Is Collidable to on to create invisible walls, floors, or barriers that prevent the player from walking through areas.

**Highlight indicators** — Use a semi-transparent Primitive to outline or highlight a region in the scene.

No unique Causes, Effects, or Traits beyond the standard Entity Spark set.

title: Step Manager
content:
# Step Manager

Step Manager structures a training experience as a named sequence of steps, each with defined completion conditions. Rather than building sequential logic from raw behavior wiring and a State Machine, Step Manager gives you a dedicated authoring surface — a visual map of your step sequence with outcome connections drawn between cards.

Step Manager is the recommended approach for procedure-based and compliance training where learners must complete tasks in a defined order.

---

## Concepts

### Steps

A step represents a stage in a training sequence. Each step has a name, an optional description, and one or more outcomes. Steps are created and managed in the "Step Manager" tab.

### Outcomes

An outcome defines a condition that, when met, advances the learner to a specified next step. Each outcome identifies the object being acted on, the condition to watch for, and the step to go to when the condition is satisfied. A step can have multiple outcomes, enabling branching paths through the sequence.

### OnEnter and OnExit

Each step is also represented as a block in the behavior tree. The block has two nodes:

- **OnEnter** — behaviors wired here fire when the step becomes active
- **OnExit** — behaviors wired here fire when the step ends, before the next step starts

Use "OnEnter" to display instructions, highlight objects, or play audio at the start of a step. Use "OnExit" to clean up — hide prompts, remove highlights, or trigger transitions. Note that "OnExit" fires only when advancing to a next step, so it never fires on the final step.

---

## Setting up Step Manager

### Add steps

1. Open the **Step Manager** tab from the top navigation bar.
2. Click **+ Add Step**. A step card appears in the canvas and a corresponding block appears in the behavior tree.
3. Name the step in the step card. Add an optional description.

Repeat for each step in your sequence. Steps appear in the list on the left as you add them. To remove a step, select it and click **- Remove Step**.

### Configure outcomes

Select a step card to open the **Step Configuration** panel on the right.

Each step starts with one outcome already in place. Configure it:

1. Set the **Object** — the Spark Instance the learner must act on. Check **All Instances** to apply the condition to every instance of that Spark rather than one specific instance.
2. Set the **Condition** — what the learner must do (see [Conditions](#conditions) below).
3. Set the **Next Step** — which step to advance to when this outcome is satisfied.

To add a second outcome (for branching paths), click **Add Outcome** and repeat the steps above.

Each outcome routes independently. If two outcomes on the same step share identical conditions, only the first outcome fires — avoid duplicating outcome conditions on the same step.

### Wire OnEnter and OnExit behaviors

In the **Behaviors** tab, locate the step block for each step. Click **Open** to expand it and access its nodes.

- Wire behaviors to **OnEnter** to execute when the step starts.
- Wire behaviors to **OnExit** to execute when the step ends, before the next step becomes active.

Any behavior wired inside a step block is only active while that step is the current step.

---

## Conditions

Each outcome requires a condition — the event that satisfies it.

| Condition | Fires when |
|---|---|
| Interacted | The learner interacts with the object (E key on desktop; laser pointer on VR controllers) |
| Collided | The learner's character collides with the object |
| Grabbed | The learner grabs the object |
| Trait Is | A specified trait on the object reaches a defined value |
| On State | A specified State Machine enters a defined state |

---

## End of sequence

When a step has no next step defined, the sequence ends. No automatic behavior occurs at completion.

**OnExit does not fire on the final step.** OnExit fires only when advancing to a next step, so the final step's OnExit node is never reached. Any end-of-training cleanup — playing audio, displaying a completion message, or advancing to another Chapter with a "Change Chapter" effect — should be wired to the final step's **OnEnter** instead.

---

## When to use Step Manager

**Use Step Manager for:**
- Compliance training where tasks must be completed in a defined order
- Procedure-based content where sequence is enforced
- Branching training where a learner's path depends on how they complete each step — add multiple outcomes to a step to route learners to different next steps based on what they did

**Use State Machine instead when:**
- Branching depends on multiple simultaneous conditions across separate state dimensions

title: Button
content:
# Button

A Button Symbol is a pressable UI element. When the user presses it, it fires the "On Button Pressed" Cause, which can wire to any downstream Effect.

---

## Causes

### On Button Pressed

Fires when the button is pressed.

---

## Effects

### Visible

Shows or hides the button.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|

### Highlight

Applies or removes the highlighted visual state on the button.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Enabled | Checked = highlighted; unchecked = normal |

### Set Interactable

Enables or disables the button's ability to receive input.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Is Interactable | Checked = button responds to input; unchecked = button is visible but cannot be pressed |

### Modify

Sets Button traits at runtime.

| Trait | Description |
|---|---|

| Highlight Color | RGBA — background color when the cursor hovers over the button |

Fires continuously as the user types. Use for real-time display or validation of input as it is entered.

# Text

A Text Symbol displays text in the UI. It can show static content (labels, instructions, signs) or be updated dynamically at runtime via behavior wiring.

title: Behaviors tab
content: # Behaviors tab The Behaviors tab is the workspace for building behavior trees — the interactive logic of a scene. It is a chapter-wide canvas showing the complete behavior graph for the entire Chapter: every behavior node from every Spark Instance of every type (Entity, Config, Symbol, and Modifier) lives on this single shared canvas. Nodes from different Spark Instances wire together freely. This is where you connect Causes to Effects. The Behaviors tab is available from both Map Editor and Map Explorer, but **behaviors only execute in play mode, which is only accessible from Map Explorer.** You can build and edit wiring from either view — but to test it, you must be in Map Explorer with play mode active. ## How the Canvas Works The Behaviors tab canvas shows all behavior nodes for the current Chapter. Nodes are not filtered to the selected Spark Instance — the whole Chapter's behavior graph is always visible. **Wiring connections** are made by dragging from an output dot at the bottom of a node to an input dot at the top of another node. Any output can connect to any input — there are no type restrictions. A chain can span multiple Spark Instances and Spark types freely. ## Adding Nodes Three dropdowns appear at the top of the Behaviors tab: **Causes**, **Effects**, and **Modifiers**. These are add menus, not filters — selecting an item and pressing **+** adds a new node to the canvas. **For Causes and Effects:** Use the Instance dropdown at the top of the panel to select the Spark Instance you want to add nodes from. The Causes and Effects dropdowns populate with that Instance's available behaviors. Select a type and press + to add it. Switch to a different Instance to add nodes from that Instance instead. **For Modifiers:** The Modifiers dropdown is not tied to the selected Instance. Modifiers belong to the Modifier Spark (described below) — select a type and press + to add it regardless of what Instance is selected. Once a node is on the canvas, the Instance dropdown has no further effect on it. Nodes already on the canvas are not filtered or hidden when you change the selected Instance. ### Selecting a Spark Instance The Instance dropdown lists every Spark Instance present in the current Chapter. You do not need to use the dropdown directly — clicking a Spark Instance anywhere in the workspace updates the dropdown automatically: - Click an Entity Spark Instance in the **Map Editor** or **Map Explorer** - Click an Instance in the **Instances pane** — the Entities, Config, or Symbols tabs in the lower right of the workspace - Click a UI element in the **UI Editor** Any of these selections drives the same Instance dropdown. Choose whichever is most convenient for your current task. If you are positioning an object in the Map Editor and want to add a behavior to it, click it there — no need to hunt through the dropdown. If you need to select a Config Spark Instance that has no visible presence in the scene, use the Config tab in the Instances pane. ## The Modifier Spark Modifiers are not behaviors of any Entity, Config, or Symbol Spark. They belong to a separate Modifier Spark that is permanently present in every Chapter — you do not add it yourself, and it cannot be removed. The Modifier Spark contains utility nodes: flow control (Delay, Toggle, Random), scene navigation (Change Chapter, Exit Book, Blackout), annotation (Comment), debugging (Debug), and others. Because Modifiers belong to the Modifier Spark rather than a specific Spark Instance, the Modifiers dropdown always shows the same options regardless of what Instance is selected. The Causes and Effects dropdowns change based on the Instance selection. The three dropdowns look parallel, but the Modifiers dropdown behaves differently from the other two. Modifier nodes appear on the shared Chapter canvas and wire into chains exactly like any other node. ## Canvas Tools A small toolbar on the left edge of the canvas provides node-level utilities: - **Copy node** — copies the selected node - **Paste node** — pastes the copied node onto the canvas - **Retarget behavior** — changes which Spark Instance a node applies to. Select a node and use this tool to reassign it to a different Instance, as long as that Instance has a compatible behavior type. ### Retargeting to reuse behavior chains If the same behavior chain repeats across multiple Spark Instances — for example, the same interaction sequence applied to several different objects — you do not have to build it from scratch each time. **Workflow:** 1. Build the chain once on the first Spark Instance. 2. Lasso-select all the nodes in the chain. 3. Copy and paste. The pasted nodes land on the canvas with all internal connections intact, still assigned to the original Instances. 4. With the pasted nodes still selected, click **Retarget behavior**. A window appears listing every Spark Instance represented in the selection — assign each one to its new target Instance and confirm. All nodes retarget in a single step. You are only changing which Instance each node belongs to; the wiring between nodes is untouched. **Constraint:** Retargeting only works if the target Instance has a compatible behavior type. For example, you can retarget an "Interacted" Cause from one Entity Spark to another Entity Spark, but not to a Config Spark that does not have that behavior. Incompatible Instances will not appear as options. ## Canvas Navigation Pan the canvas by holding the middle mouse button and dragging, or by right-clicking and dragging. Scroll to zoom. **Zoom to Fit All** centers the view on the entire Chapter graph. **Zoom to Fit Selected** centers the view on whatever nodes are currently selected. Both are especially useful when you open a Chapter and the canvas appears empty — nodes may exist far off-screen from where the view happens to start. Click **Zoom to Fit All** and the canvas will jump to wherever the nodes actually are. If you have specific nodes selected, **Zoom to Fit Selected** narrows the view to just those. ## Chapter Started "Chapter Started" is a special Modifier node that fires once when the Chapter loads, before any learner interaction. It is found in the Modifiers section, not in Causes, because it belongs to the Modifier Spark rather than any Instance. Use it as the starting point for initialization behaviors that must run at Chapter load — setting positions, establishing visibility states, or triggering audio that plays as the scene opens. For a detailed explanation, see [Edit Mode vs. Play Mode](../../../getting-started/edit-mode-and-play-mode/), which covers when and why to use Chapter Started.

title: Gizmo
content:
# Gizmo

The Gizmo is the transform control that appears when you select a Spark Instance in the Map Editor or Map Explorer. It lets you move, rotate, and scale the selected Instance directly in the viewport using color-coded handles — no mode switching required.

| Handle | Color | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Lines | Red, green, blue | Drag to move along a single axis |
| Squares | Red, green, blue | Drag to move within a plane (two axes simultaneously) |
| Arc | Green | Drag to rotate |
| Center box | White | Drag to scale uniformly (fixed ratio) |

The Gizmo always scales proportionally — there is no handle for non-uniform scaling. To set different scale values on individual axes, enter them directly in the Traits Panel.

For numeric precision on any transform, use the Traits Panel — enter exact values for Position, Altitude, Rotation, and Scale rather than dragging the Gizmo handles. The Gizmo is faster for approximate placement; the Traits Panel is more reliable for exact values.

title: Map Editor
content:
# Map Editor

The Map Editor is a construction view with a fixed camera for placing and positioning Spark Instances with precision. Use it when you are building and arranging your scene — placing objects, aligning them, and checking spatial relationships from consistent angles.

The Map Editor is for building. The Map Explorer is for testing. They show the same scene from different vantage points and with different tools available.

## Camera Orientations

The Map Editor offers seven camera orientations accessible from its toolbar:

| Orientation | What you see |
|---|---|
| Top Down | Looking straight down onto the scene floor |
| Bottom Up | Looking straight up from below the scene |
| North-South | Looking from north toward south |
| South-North | Looking from south toward north |
| East-West | Looking from east toward west |
| West-East | Looking from west toward east |
| Fly Cam | Free movement — position and angle the camera freely |

Switch between orientations to place Spark Instances accurately on all axes. A common workflow: use Top Down to set horizontal placement, then switch to North-South or East-West to adjust height.

## Snap

When Snap is enabled, Spark Instances move in grid increments rather than freely. Use Snap when precise alignment matters — for example, placing objects flush against walls or aligning objects to a shared baseline. Disable Snap when you need freeform placement.

## X-Ray Mode

X-Ray Mode moves the camera along a selected axis and cuts through the scene at that plane, making objects behind other objects visible. Use it when you need to see inside a complex scene — for example, viewing the interior of a machine or checking placement inside an enclosed space. X-Ray Mode affects the view only; it does not change the scene.

## Zoom Shortcuts

Two zoom shortcuts are available:

- **Zoom to Player** — moves the camera to the player's current position in the scene
- **Zoom to Selected** — moves the camera to focus on the currently selected Spark Instance

Use these to quickly navigate to a specific location without manually repositioning the camera.

## Navigation Controls

Camera controls differ between fixed camera modes and Fly Cam.

**Fixed camera modes (Top Down, Bottom Up, North-South, South-North, East-West, West-East):**

| Control | Action |
|---|---|
| Right-click + drag | Pan within the camera plane |
| Scroll wheel | Zoom in / out |

**Fly Cam:**

| Control | Action |
|---|---|
| W / A / S / D | Move camera (relative to current camera orientation) |
| Left-click + drag | Look around (rotate camera) |
| E | Move camera up |
| Q | Move camera down |
| Scroll wheel | Zoom in / out |

These are camera controls — you are moving and orienting the editor camera, not an avatar.

## Behaviors in Map Editor

Behaviors are never active in Map Editor. Wiring in the Behaviors tab exists and can be edited, but nothing executes. To test behaviors, switch to Map Explorer and enter play mode.

`[PENDING: implementation mid-April. Currently behaviors can fire outside of play mode — this is a known issue and is on the requirements list to fix before trial launch. The doc describes post-fix behavior.]`

title: Map Explorer
content:
# Map Explorer

The Map Explorer is a player-perspective view of the scene. The camera is attached to the player character. Use Map Explorer when you want to experience the scene the way a learner would — walking through it, testing interactions, and running behavior trees.

The Map Explorer is for testing and experiencing. The Map Editor is for constructing.

## Navigation Controls

Move through the scene using keyboard and mouse:

| Control | Action |
|---|---|
| W / A / S / D or Arrow Keys | Move forward, left, back, right |
| Right-click + drag (two-finger click + drag on Mac trackpad) | Look around |
| E | Interact with an object *(play mode only)* |
| R | Grab an object *(play mode only)* |
| Space *(gravity off only)* | Move up |
| Option / Alt *(gravity off only)* | Move down |

Space and Option/Alt for vertical movement are only active when the physics toggle (gravity) is off. With gravity on, Space has no effect in Map Explorer.

The Interact (E) and Grab (R) keys trigger object behaviors. These only have effect in play mode — pressing them outside of play mode does nothing.

## Camera and View Modes

Map Explorer has a view mode dropdown in the toolbar that controls the camera perspective:

| Mode | Projection | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Fly Cam | Perspective | Free-movement camera; navigate the scene as a player would |
| Top Down | Orthographic | Looking straight down from above |
| Bottom Up | Orthographic | Looking straight up from below |
| North to South | Orthographic | Side view along the North–South axis |
| South to North | Orthographic | Opposite side view |
| East to West | Orthographic | Side view along the East–West axis |
| West to East | Orthographic | Opposite side view |

Fixed views (everything except Fly Cam) use orthographic projection — no perspective distortion, useful for precise alignment checking. Fly Cam uses perspective projection, which matches how the scene will appear to players.

You can rotate the camera freely in any view mode outside of play mode. Camera rotation in Map Explorer is independent from the camera in Map Editor — changing the view in one does not affect the other.

The default camera for player experience is **first person** — you see from the player's eye level. Third person is also available and can be changed in the Book settings. First person is the expected perspective for VR training content and is the appropriate default for most scenes.

## Testing Controls

Three buttons appear at the top of the Map Explorer viewport:

- **Physics toggle** — turns player physics (gravity, collision) on or off. Toggle physics off if you want to move through walls or fly through the scene without constraint during testing.
- **Reload Chapter** — reloads the current Chapter from saved state, including all Spark Instances and behavior trees. Use this to reset the scene during a test session without leaving Map Explorer.
- **Start Chapter** — launches the full Chapter experience as if a learner opened it. Use this to do a complete run-through from the beginning.

## Play Mode

Play mode is only available in Map Explorer. The **play button (triangle icon)** is in the bottom-right corner of the Map Explorer viewport. Clicking it enters play mode — all wired behaviors become active and respond to interaction. The button turns purple when play mode is active. To exit play mode, click the button again. If you have unsaved changes when you enter play mode, Builder will prompt you to save first.

This means Map Editor is always in edit mode. There is no way to run behaviors from Map Editor. If behaviors are not responding during testing, verify you are in Map Explorer with play mode active.

For a complete explanation of how edit mode and play mode differ and what each is for, see [Edit Mode vs. Play Mode](../../../getting-started/edit-mode-and-play-mode/).

**Note:** A "Reset on Stop" checkbox currently appears in Map Explorer but has no effect. The checkbox will be removed in a future update — ignore it.

> **Wait for all loading indicators to clear before interacting.** When a Chapter is loading, one or more loading popups appear on screen. If you attempt to interact with the scene before all of them have finished, the application can get stuck. Wait until the loading UI is fully gone before navigating or triggering behaviors.

title: Spark Browser
content:
# Spark Browser

The Spark Browser is your library of everything available to place in a scene. All Sparks — Entity, Config, Symbol, and Environment — are organized here in folders. You drag Sparks from the browser into the Map Editor or Map Explorer to create Spark Instances.

Everything you add to a scene begins here.

### Browsing and Finding Sparks

Sparks are organized in top-level folders by type:

- **Entity Sparks** — 3D objects you place in the scene
- **Config Sparks** — logic and configuration elements with no physical presence
- **Symbol Sparks** — 2D interface elements used in UI Panels

Within each folder, Sparks are organized into subfolders. Browse by expanding folders. To place a Spark, drag it from the browser into the Map Editor or into the Map Explorer viewport.

**Environment Sparks** currently appear as their own top-level folder alongside Entity, Config, and Symbol Sparks. Environment Sparks are technically a subtype of Entity Spark — this placement is recognized as potentially misleading. A UI cleanup to move Environment Sparks inside the Entity Sparks folder is planned before trial launch.

**My Sparks** is a personal folder where Sparks you have created or imported are stored. It is separate from the built-in Spark library and is yours to organize as needed.

### Search

The Spark Browser has a search field. Searching returns matching Sparks by name. **Search results show the Spark name only — they do not show the folder path.** If you need to know where a Spark lives in the folder hierarchy, browse to it manually. The ability to show the folder path in search results is a planned feature.

### Organizing Your Sparks

Within My Sparks, you can create folders to organize your Sparks:

- **"Create Local Directory"** — creates a folder inside My Sparks. This is a standard folder for organization only — it has no special file system behavior. A rename to "New Folder" is under consideration.
- **"Export Spark"** — saves a Spark to any location on your local drive. Low expected usage — the primary reason to use this is sharing a Spark file with another author outside of platform sync.

### Asset Config

The "Asset Config" button in the Spark Browser is a placeholder for an upcoming feature: an org-specific asset library that will let your organization's custom assets appear directly in the browser. It does not currently route to an active destination. You can safely ignore it.

title: Traits Panel
content:
# Traits Panel

The Traits Panel shows the configurable properties of the currently selected Spark Instance. Every Spark Instance has traits — values that define how it looks, behaves, and participates in behavior trees.

Select a Spark Instance in the Map Editor or Map Explorer to see its traits here.

> **Multi-select clears the panel.** If more than one Spark Instance is selected, the Traits Panel shows nothing. To view or edit traits, select one Instance at a time.

## What Traits Are

Traits are instance-specific property overrides. A Spark defines a set of properties as a template; a Spark Instance inherits those properties but can have individual values that differ from the template default. Changes made in the Traits Panel apply only to the selected Instance — they do not affect the Spark definition or any other Instance of the same Spark.

Common traits for Entity Spark Instances include:

- **Is Visible** — whether the object is visible when the Chapter loads
- **Is Interactable** — whether the player can activate the object with the laser pointer
- **Is Grabbable** — whether the player can pick up the object
- **Is Collidable** — whether physics collisions are registered for this object
- **Position, Altitude, Rotation, Scale** — the object's transform in the scene

Other Sparks expose different traits. A Config Spark like a State Machine exposes its defined states and starting state. An Audio Config Spark exposes its audio file and channel settings.

## Editing Traits Directly

You can type values directly into any trait field in the Traits Panel. Click the field and enter the value — the change applies immediately to the selected Instance.

This is the primary way to set precise values. The Gizmo lets you move, rotate, and scale objects by dragging in the scene, which is useful for rough placement and spatial judgment. When you need an exact number — a specific position coordinate, a rotation of exactly 90 degrees, a scale of 0.5 — type it directly into the Traits Panel.

**Position, Rotation, and Scale** are the most common traits edited this way. Each is exposed as individual X, Y, and Z fields. Common use cases:

- Snapping an object to a known coordinate after rough placement with the Gizmo
- Recording the exact coordinates of two positions to use later in a Move Effect
- Setting uniform scale across all axes without relying on drag handles
- Resetting rotation to zero after adjusting orientation in the scene

The two approaches are complementary. Use the Gizmo to get an object roughly where you want it, then use the Traits Panel to dial in the exact values.

## Replacing the Underlying Spark

> **Known issue (PLATFORM-2203):** Swapping the Base Spark currently leaves the replacement Instance invisible and non-interactive in both the Map Editor and Map Explorer. Placing the same Spark fresh from the Spark Browser works correctly — the swap path specifically is affected. Until this is fixed, do not rely on the Base Spark swap; delete the old Instance and place the new Spark fresh instead.

The **Base Spark** field sits at the top of the Traits Panel and shows the name of the Spark that defines the currently selected Spark Instance. You can use it to swap a Spark Instance onto a different Spark definition without re-placing the Instance or rewiring its behaviors.

This is different from **Retarget behavior** in the Behaviors tab. Retarget behavior reassigns an individual Cause or Effect node to a different Spark Instance — the Instances themselves are untouched. Replacing the Base Spark changes which Spark an Instance is built from — the Instance stays in place, but everything it inherits from its Spark (its mesh or UI layout, its available traits, its Cause and Effect definitions) comes from the new Spark instead. See [Behaviors tab](behaviors-tab.md) for Retarget behavior.

### How to swap a Spark

1. Select the Spark Instance you want to change. Its current Spark name appears in the Base Spark field.
2. Drag a Spark from the Spark Browser onto the Base Spark field.
3. Builder applies the swap immediately — no confirmation step.

The Instance keeps its place in the Chapter. Its Instance name, Instance ID, position, and wired behaviors carry over onto the new Spark. Only the underlying Spark definition changes.

### Same type only

Builder restricts the swap to a new Spark that is the same Spark class as the current one, or a subtype of it. For example, if the selected Instance is built from a Cube Spark, you can drop another Cube Spark on it, but not a Sphere Spark — even though both are Entity Sparks. Sharing a broad category (Entity, Config, Symbol) is not sufficient; the new Spark's class has to match or specialize the current one.

Dropping an incompatible Spark, or dropping a Map, does nothing — Builder rejects the drop silently rather than swapping.

### What carries over, and what doesn't

- **Carries over:** Instance name, Instance ID, wired Causes and Effects, and every trait value the new Spark also exposes by the same trait definition — including Position, Altitude, Rotation, and Scale.
- **Does not carry over:** the underlying Spark file reference. After the swap, the Instance points at the new Spark's file, not the old one.
- **Trait values with no match on the new Spark are dropped.** If the new Spark doesn't expose a trait the old one did, that value is discarded rather than failing the swap.
- **Wiring with no match on the new Spark is dropped.** If the new Spark doesn't define an equivalent Cause or Effect, any behavior wired to that node is left disconnected rather than failing the swap.

**Position, Rotation, and Scale transfer as raw numbers, not as a visual match.** Because Position, Altitude, Rotation, and Scale are traits, the swap carries over the exact values from the old Instance — it does not recalculate them for the new Spark's mesh size or pivot point. If the new Spark has different dimensions or a different pivot than the old one, the Instance can end up the wrong size, floating, or partially embedded in the floor at the same trait values that looked correct on the old Spark. Check the Instance in the Map Editor after any swap and adjust Position or Scale if needed.

## Traits and the Behaviors tab

Several Causes in the Behaviors tab require a corresponding trait to be enabled before they can fire. The Grabbed Cause requires Is Grabbable. The Interacted Cause requires Is Interactable. The Collided Cause requires Is Collidable.

**If a Cause is not firing, check the Traits Panel first.** A Cause whose prerequisite trait is disabled will fail silently in most cases — the behavior tree runs but nothing happens. Verifying traits directly is always faster than debugging the behavior tree first.

## Traits and Edit Mode

In edit mode, trait values in the Traits Panel represent the starting state of the scene. What you see in the Traits Panel is what a learner sees when the Chapter loads. If you modify a trait during testing in play mode, that change is not saved — when you exit play mode, the trait returns to its edit mode value.

title: UI Editor
content:
# UI Editor

The UI Editor is the authoring workspace for building 2D interface content displayed on a Billboard Spark Instance. Use it to design the flat UI layer — buttons, text, images, and other Symbol Spark elements — that a Billboard shows in the 3D scene.

The UI Editor is only active when a Billboard Spark Instance is selected in the dropdown at the upper right of the panel.

## Step 1 — Add a Billboard to the Scene

Open the Spark Browser and navigate to **Symbols / UI Containers**. You will find two Billboard types:

- **Billboard** — placed at a fixed position in world space. The learner must be facing it to see it.
- **Follow Head Billboard** — attached to the learner's view and always visible regardless of where they are in the environment. Use this for persistent HUD elements or instructions that must always be readable.

Drag the Billboard type you want into the scene from the Spark Browser, or drop it directly into the Map Explorer.

**Rename the Instance immediately.** Scenes with multiple Billboards become difficult to manage if they all have default names. Set a descriptive Instance Name in the Traits Panel as soon as the Billboard is placed.

## Step 2 — Configure Billboard Traits

With the Billboard Instance selected, the Traits Panel shows several configuration options:

**Canvas Resolution (X, Y)** — sets the pixel dimensions of the Billboard's surface. This controls the resolution of the 2D canvas, not the physical size of the object in the scene. Default is 1920 × 1080. Adjust the physical size using the Scale trait or the Gizmo.

**Background Color** — sets the background color of the Billboard canvas.

**Rotate towards camera** — when enabled, the Billboard automatically rotates so its front face always points at the player's camera. Useful for Billboards placed in the scene that should always be readable regardless of where the player is standing.

**Lock X Auto-Rotate / Lock Y Auto-Rotate** — constrains the auto-rotation axis when Rotate towards camera is enabled. Locking the X axis is the most common setting: the Billboard can spin horizontally to face the player but will not tilt up or down. Locking Y prevents horizontal rotation while allowing tilt.

**Rotation** — for a standard Billboard (Rotate towards camera disabled), you will need to set rotation manually. Billboards only display content on one face, and it can be difficult to tell which side is the front when the canvas is empty. Consider adding a Symbol Spark first so the front face becomes visible, then adjust rotation.

## Step 3 — Open the UI Editor

Click the **UI Editor** tab in the top navigation bar. In the upper right of the UI Editor panel, a dropdown lists every Billboard Instance in the current Chapter. Select the Billboard you want to edit. The canvas for that Billboard appears in the editor.

**Hidden Billboard gotcha:** If a Billboard's visibility is set to hidden in the scene, it will also be invisible in the UI Editor — you will see a blank canvas with no content visible to interact with. To edit a hidden Billboard, use the **Is Visible** toggle in the upper left of the UI Editor (this is a shortcut to set the Billboard's visibility trait to true). Make your edits, then remember to re-hide the Billboard when you are done. This is a known issue with no current fix scheduled.

## Step 4 — Add and Arrange Symbol Sparks

With a Billboard selected in the UI Editor dropdown, the Spark Browser displays the Symbol Sparks library. Drag Symbol Sparks from the browser directly onto the Billboard canvas. Once placed, you can:

- **Move** — drag the element to reposition it on the canvas
- **Resize** — drag the handles to scale the element
- **Select** — click to select and edit properties in the Traits Panel

Symbol Sparks placed in the UI Editor become Instances tracked in the Symbols tab of the Instances pane, the same as any other Spark Instance.

**Image backgrounds:** To use an image as a background or decorative element on a Billboard, import the image as an **ImageViewer Spark**. See *(ImageViewer Spark reference — forthcoming)* for import details.

## Step 5 — Wire Behaviors

Switch to the **Behaviors tab** to wire Causes and Effects for the Symbol Spark Instances on the Billboard. The UI Editor handles layout and composition; the Behaviors tab handles interactive logic. Neither alone is sufficient to build an interactive UI element.

For example: to make a button navigate to the next Chapter, select the Button Instance in the Behaviors tab, add an **On Button Pressed** Cause, and wire it to a **Change Chapter** Effect.

Causes, Effects, and parameters specific to each Symbol Spark type are documented in the individual Symbol Spark reference pages.

> **Interacting with UI buttons is different from interacting with Entity Sparks.** In Builder play mode (and in the published experience), UI buttons on a Billboard respond to a **mouse click** — move the cursor over the button and click. They do not respond to the **E key**, which is reserved for Entity Sparks with Is Interactable enabled. In VR, the laser pointer trigger activates both UI buttons and interactable Entity Sparks, so this distinction only affects desktop play.
